title: Judge orders trial in Charlie Kirk shooting; death penalty possible
dek: Judge Tony Graf ruled that Tyler James Robinson, 23, must stand trial on aggravated murder charges in the September 10, 2025 shooting death of conservative activist Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University. The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the death penalty after finding sufficient evidence and that others' lives were knowingly endangered during the shooting.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Judge Graf found sufficient evidence that Robinson was aware of people positioned near Kirk when he fired, overriding defense arguments that he had a single, clear shot at Kirk specifically.
bottom_line: Robinson is scheduled to appear in court on October 23, 2026, when a trial date is expected to be set. The trial will test whether the prosecution's video, DNA, and witness evidence meets the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt, and whether the "great risk of death" finding will survive any later challenges that could determine whether the death penalty remains available.
body:
Judge Tony Graf ruled on September 2 that Tyler James Robinson, 23, must stand trial on aggravated murder charges in the September 10, 2025 shooting death of conservative activist Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. The ruling allows prosecutors to pursue the death penalty, life imprisonment without parole, or 25 years to life with parole eligibility, according to CBS News.
Kirk, 31, the co-founder of the conservative student organization Turning Point USA, was shot in the neck while speaking at an outdoor rally at Utah Valley University. According to ABC News, Robinson is accused of firing the shot from a rooftop approximately 415 feet from where Kirk was speaking. Robinson has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
Judge Graf's decision rested on his finding that Robinson was aware of people positioned near Kirk when he fired. The judge stated: "These circumstances support a reasonable inference that defendant was aware that other individuals were positioned near Mr. Kirk when he fired," according to CBS News. This determination was critical because it establishes the "great risk of death" aggravating factor that makes the offense eligible for capital punishment.
Prosecutors presented evidence during a five-day July hearing that Robinson shot Kirk because he disagreed with him by firing into a crowd of thousands, according to CBS News. Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court: "There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," citing video footage, DNA evidence on the suspected murder weapon, and alleged admissions by Robinson, per BBC News reporting. McBride outlined video showing Robinson "dressed to kill" on campus on the day of the shooting, according to BBC News.
Physical evidence cited by prosecutors includes Robinson's DNA found on his grandfather's rifle, which was stashed in a wooded area near campus after the shooting, as well as on a towel the rifle was wrapped in and a screwdriver recovered at the scene, according to BBC News. Engravings found on casings from the shooting allegedly matched a Dremel tool recovered at the home Robinson shared with his roommate, per BBC News.
Robinson's roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs, provided a videotaped interview with prosecutors and detectives in which he claimed Robinson confessed to killing Kirk in a letter, text messages, and in person, according to BBC News. Twiggs testified that Robinson cried and said he wished he had not done it. Robinson turned himself in the day after the murder, accompanied by his family and a neighbor, per BBC News.
Prosecutors argued Robinson was motivated by political disagreement with Kirk and alleged that he knew children were present and would witness the shooting. According to BBC News, prosecutors said Robinson regarded Kirk's conservative views, particularly on transgender issues, as "repugnant." Prosecutor Chad Grunander stated: "He was playing, in effect, a game of ballistic roulette. It's been 356 days since Tyler Robinson assassinated Charlie Kirk. It's time for him, the defendant, to be bound over for trial and arraigned. Today," per BBC News. Prosecutors told the court: "Prosecutors say you can't shoot a rifle into a crowd of 3,000 people and not know that you are posing a significant risk of death," according to CBS News.
Defense attorney Staci Visser asked the judge to strike the "great risk of death" aggravating factor, arguing it is not supported by the facts of the case. Visser stated: "There's nothing in this evidence showing that there was a great risk that someone else was going to be killed," according to ABC News. Defense attorney Richard Novak raised questions about political motivation, stating: "There's no evidence as to really what was in Mr. Robinson's mind, if in fact he was the shooter, about Charlie Kirk, because we have no testimony that Mr. Robinson had ever spoken about Charlie Kirk, that he had ever heard anything he'd said, that he'd ever discussed anything," per ABC News. Defense lawyers also raised procedural objections regarding expert credentials and repeatedly objected to cameras livestreaming court proceedings, according to BBC News.
The obstruction charge carries a penalty of up to 15 years in jail, while felony discharge carries five years to life in prison, according to CBS News. Judge Graf ordered Robinson to stand trial on all seven counts. Not guilty pleas were entered on Robinson's behalf following the ruling, per ABC News.
Kirk's family issued a statement: "Today's decision, which comes nearly a year since Charlie was taken from us, marks an important step in our family's pursuit of justice for him. Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," according to CBS News.
Robinson's mother, Amber Robinson, watched from the courtroom gallery, while his father, Matt Robinson, listened with his head bowed, according to CBS News. Robinson had no visible reaction to the arguments.
